newsitem.title: Switzerland: UN envoy says concerned over jailed Ogoni leaders.
newsitem.headline: UN envoy says concerned over jailed Ogoni leaders.

text.p: A U.N. human rights investigator who goes to Nigeria this month expressed concern on Friday over the plight of 19 jailed Ogoni leaders who were close to the executed writer Ken Saro-Wiwa and also face the death penalty.

In an interview, Param Cumaraswamy, U.N. special rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers, said that he and Bacre Waly Ndiaye, U.N. special rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions, hoped to visit Moshood Abiola.
"We have received a large number of allegations over the last two years. The mission is to give us an opportunity to see for ourselves to what extent they are true," he told Reuters.
"My colleague (Ndiaye) has received allegations of extrajudicial killings," Cumaraswamy added.
The two have asked to see Abiola, the presidential claimant who has been jailed on charges of treason since June 1994 after a previous army government annulled a 1993 presidential poll.
"We have asked for access to all prisons and detention centres and access to meet him," Cumaraswamy said in Geneva.
"We have been assured by the government and the ambassador here that we will have no restrictions imposed on us," he said of Abiola, adding: "We therefore hope to meet him."
The two envoys will travel to Nigeria at the invitation of the government from February 23 to March 5, and plan to report back to the U.N. Commission on Human Rights the following week.
They hope to see detained pro-democracy opposition figures as well as 19 Ogoni leaders being held in Port Harcourt.

Nigeria drew worldwide outrage in November 1995 when it hanged Saro-Wiwa and eight Ogoni minority rights activists after their conviction in the 1994 murder of four pro-government tribal chiefs. Their trial was judged unfair by international judicial experts, but the defendants had no right to appeal.
They had been campaigning for compensation for Ogoniland in south-eastern Nigeria for oil produced there by multi-national corporations. The 19 are also charged with the four murders.

"Since the execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa and the eight Ogonis we have been wanting to make a visit to Nigeria, to see for ourselves the state of human rights and in particular matters pertaining to our respective mandates," Cumaraswamy said, adding: "We hope something positive will turn out at the end."

"After what happened in the tragic episode of Ken Saro-Wiwa, we are concerned about the state of judicial independence and want of due process in Nigeria in trials of those who are arrested and detained.

"We are concerned about the plight of Ogonis who are detained and still not brought to trial," he added. "They should be tried as soon as possible if there is evidence against them, otherwise they should be released. In the meantime, they should be provided with adequate medical attention."
The 19 Ogoni, said to be detained in poor conditions and in deteriorating health, were followers of Saro-Wiwa and belonged to the Movement to Save the Ogoni People (MOSOP).
Cumaraswamy, a Malaysian lawyer, expressed concern over the large number of special courts in Nigeria for certain offences.
"We are concerned about all those wrongly detained or detained for long periods of time without being brought to trial. We assert that trials must be open and before ordinary courts."
Amnesty International, the International Commission of Jurists and Human Rights Watch were among the non-governmental organisations which have provided the envoys with reports.
A U.N. statement announcing the visit made clear that the investigators expected full access to detainees and dissidents.

After both U.N. investigators hold talks in Lagos and Abuja, Ndiaye will be going to Kano and Kaduna in the north. Cumaraswamy will head south to Port Harcourt in the same state as oil-rich Ogoniland, where he hopes to check on the 19 Ogoni.
Nigeria will be one of the countries in the dock when the main U.N. human rights forum opens its annual six-week meeting in Geneva on March 10, according to U.N. sources.
